messages.author: 7347479aef4e9693
messages.subject: Incorporating species-specific variables in MSOMs
parts:
Hello,

I’m hoping for some advice on a question that’s been on my mind. I’m fitting MSOMs for four co-occurring species and I want to include a species-specific independent variable (connectivity) in my model. For each species, connectivity is measured as the proportion of the surrounding area (within maximum dispersal distance) that consists of marsh habitat that is at least the size of the species' minimum home range.

Here’s where I’m stuck:

  1. Is it okay to include species-specific variables like this in an MSOM, or does that defeat the purpose of the model?
  2. If it is possible, how do I go about incorporating these into my model? 
  3. Can I still use species-specific variables in interaction terms (e.g., to explore the interaction between area and connectivity on occupancy)?

Thanks in advance for your help!

messages.author: 7347479aef4e9693
messages.subject: Re: Incorporating species-specific variables in MSOMs
parts:
Follow-up question: I found during my exploratory analysis that my connectivity variables are correlated. I reduced these down to a single principal component, but am not sure if this is an appropriate approach since these are species-specific variables and I expect them to have differing effects on occupancy. Would it be better to keep them all in my models despite their collinearity and instead:
  1. Include a random intercept for species to account for species variability, and/or
              e.g., stateformulas <- list(psi ~ connectivity + area + connectivity:area + (1|species))
    ​
  2. Model random slopes for connectivity to capture species-specific variations in occupancy 
             e.g., stateformulas <- list(psi ~ connectivity + area + connectivity:area + (1 + connectivity|species))
I'm sure there are other options for handling the data (if including unique connectivity values is even a valid option) and I am open to other suggestions as well. Thanks!

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incorporating species-specific variables in MSOMs
parts:
You can use species-specific covariates. Whether it makes sense really depends on your understanding of the system. It definitely would make sense to me to include a species-specific covariate on the relevant first order term for that species in the Rota model. I'm less sure if such a covariate makes sense on a two-species interaction term but I think it is possible. It really depends on the exact hypothesis you are testing.

Regarding your other question about correlation, I'm not sure. What I can say is that occuMulti does not support random effects at this time (unlike some other unmarked functions) so that particular option would not be possible.

Ken

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incorporating species-specific variables in MSOMs
parts:
spOccupancy cannot fit the Rota-type multispecies occupancy model. It fits a community occupancy model without species interactions. That said, if that is what you need, it is a great package. As far as I know it is also somewhat limited in the random effects structure it supports.

If you need complex random effects, your best choice is probably to code the model yourself in JAGS/Nimble or Stan.

Ken

messages.author: f0e02cc3862562f5
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incorporating species-specific variables in MSOMs
parts:
Just to add to Ken's response. I would say it's not only possible to include species-specific variables in the first order models, but critical to getting meaningful inference from these models into co-occurrence of species. If you have unmodeled heterogeneity in occupancy, this is soaked up by the interaction terms, and so can be problematic if a missing covariate impacts both species (for example, if both species respond positively to covariate x, and you do not include it in the first order models, and you fit a constant interaction on f12, this will result a positive interaction term being estimated erroneously). Good to be cognizant of this in any interpretation of these models. 

Species-specific covariates on the interaction terms would seem less obviously justified (but it really depends on what the hypotheses you are testing is). I don't understand what you mean by "to explore the interaction between area and connectivity on occupancy" but fitting habitat covariates on interaction terms models heterogeneity in co-occurrence as a function of that covariate (distinct from the species' individual responses to that covariate, which you fit in the first order models).

 It is also worth considering the sample size requirements of these models - these models require a lot of data to support them (even for simple constant interaction terms, recent preprint by Cowans et al. suggest >400 sites when co-occurrence is strong), fitting covariates on interaction terms is very costly in terms of sampling requirements,

Josh
On Thu, Jan 2, 2025 at 10:14 AM Kristin Brandon <kbrandon...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thank you. It seems like I will have to figure out a way to make this work in unmarked as I am unfamiliar with JAGS/Nimble and Stan and working on a tight deadline. I appreciate your help with this!

On Thursday, January 2, 2025 at 8:43:21 AM UTC-8 Ken Kellner wrote:
spOccupancy cannot fit the Rota-type multispecies occupancy model. It fits a community occupancy model without species interactions. That said, if that is what you need, it is a great package. As far as I know it is also somewhat limited in the random effects structure it supports.

If you need complex random effects, your best choice is probably to code the model yourself in JAGS/Nimble or Stan.

Ken
